proposals.name: QUESTION FIT
proposals.rationale: Manual awards favor answers that solve the asker’s actual problem rather than merely displaying mathematical ability.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the answer targets the exact mathematical task and its stated constraints; low when it mainly addresses a neighboring question. Does not apply when the question itself is underspecified.

proposals.name: CONCEPTUAL INSIGHT
proposals.rationale: Insight helps distinguish a genuinely valuable solution from technically correct but interchangeable manipulation.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the answer exposes the underlying mechanism, invariant, or idea making the result work; low when it only performs procedures. Does not apply when the task is purely computational.

proposals.name: METHOD REUSABILITY
proposals.rationale: Reusable methods provide broader value and are plausible targets for deliberate bounty selection.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the approach can be adapted to a recognizable class of related problems; low when it is tied narrowly to one instance. Does not apply to deliberately one-off questions.

proposals.name: DECISIVE RESOLUTION
proposals.rationale: A manual award decision generally favors answers that settle the requested mathematical issue.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the answer reaches an explicit, unambiguous conclusion answering the question; low when it leaves the central issue unresolved. Does not apply when the question explicitly requests exploration only.

proposals.name: ASSUMPTION MANAGEMENT
proposals.rationale: Careful management of assumptions makes an answer safer to endorse and reward.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the answer identifies and handles conventions, hidden hypotheses, or exceptional cases that affect its conclusion; low when it silently relies on them. Does not apply when no meaningful assumptions are present.

proposals.name: LIMITATION DISCLOSURE
proposals.rationale: Honest calibration is a quality signal for considered human judgment.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the answer explicitly distinguishes proved claims from conjectures, guesses, citations, or unverified extensions; low when it presents them interchangeably. Does not apply when every claim is elementary and established within the response.

proposals.name: ERROR SELF-CORRECTION
proposals.rationale: Visible self-correction can demonstrate substantive engagement and improve award-worthiness.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the answer notices, repairs, or sharply qualifies an earlier mistake; low when apparent errors remain unacknowledged. Does not apply when the response introduces no prior attempt or correction.

proposals.name: COUNTEREXAMPLE SENSITIVITY
proposals.rationale: Counterexample awareness separates robust mathematical judgment from superficial pattern matching.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the answer tests its claim against plausible boundary cases or counterexamples; low when it makes broad claims without such checks. Does not apply when the statement’s domain excludes meaningful alternatives.

proposals.name: ANSWER ECONOMY
proposals.rationale: Efficient relevance makes a strong answer easier for a bounty-setter to identify and select.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the response allocates attention to the central task without ornamental digressions; low when substantial space is irrelevant to the requested result. Does not apply when broad exposition is explicitly requested.

proposals.name: APPROACH DISTINCTIVENESS
proposals.rationale: Distinctive contribution is a plausible reason a manual selector chooses one answer over competitors.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the response offers a genuinely distinctive route, viewpoint, or synthesis visible in the text; low when it merely repeats a routine template. Does not apply when the problem specifically demands a standard method.

proposals.name: STRUCTURAL DECOMPOSITION
proposals.rationale: Strategic decomposition signals deliberate problem-solving value beyond surface fluency.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the answer breaks a difficult problem into strategically meaningful subproblems; low when steps are mechanically listed without revealing their roles. Does not apply to problems already atomic.

proposals.name: RESULT INTERPRETATION
proposals.rationale: Interpretation helps a human judge recognize why the response matters.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the answer explains what its calculation or theorem means for the original question; low when it stops at an uninterpreted expression. Does not apply when the requested output is solely a raw value.

proposals.name: CONNECTION BUILDING
proposals.rationale: Meaningful connections increase intellectual value without reducing to ordinary exposition.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the answer connects the problem to a relevant theorem, analogy, or broader mathematical structure and explains the connection; low when references are merely name-dropped. Does not apply when no useful connection exists.

proposals.name: EXECUTABLE PROCEDURE
proposals.rationale: Actionable answers are easier to judge as genuinely solving the posed task.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when a reader could carry out the proposed construction, algorithm, or verification from the answer; low when it only gestures toward one. Does not apply when the question asks only for existence or intuition.

proposals.name: SCOPE PROPORTIONALITY
proposals.rationale: Proportionate effort helps explain why a human would deliberately choose this answer for the bounty.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the answer’s ambition and technical detail match the question’s scope; low when it substantially under-answers or over-engineers the task. Does not apply when the question explicitly requests maximal generality.

proposals.name: Answer length
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Approximate the answer’s total prose, displayed mathematics, and sections.

proposals.name: Display-math density
proposals.parent: who answers this kind of question
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Estimate the proportion of the answer occupied by displayed equations or formulas.

proposals.name: Citation-and-link density
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Count named authors, papers, books, websites, URLs, or formal bibliographic references.

proposals.name: Bounty-meta language
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Note explicit references to bounties, awarding, accepting, or competing answers.

proposals.name: Cross-answer references
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Identify mentions of other answers, users, comments, edits, or “another approach.”

proposals.name: Temporal self-markers
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Identify phrases such as “years later,” “next month,” “after studying,” or other posting-time cues.

proposals.name: Credential or affiliation cues
proposals.parent: who answers this kind of question
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Note references to a thesis, course, colleague, students, institution, or professional role.

proposals.name: Personal disclaimer boilerplate
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Count stock phrases expressing uncertainty, gratitude, apology, or requests to check the work.

proposals.name: Raw markup artifacts
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Note unrendered HTML, verbatim commands, custom macros, malformed delimiters, or code-like formatting.

proposals.name: Specialized topic vocabulary
proposals.parent: who answers this kind of question
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Estimate how concentrated the answer is in advanced terminology from a recognizable mathematical subfield.

proposals.name: Thread-aware engagement
proposals.rationale: Manual awards can favor answers that visibly resolve the thread’s particular unresolved issue.
proposals.description: Scores high when the answer responds to specific prior answers, comments, or discussion gaps; low when it reads as generic. Does not apply when no thread context appears.

proposals.name: Question-specific tailoring
proposals.rationale: Deliberate selection is more plausible when an answer is visibly shaped around this question.
proposals.description: Scores high when notation, examples, or methods are adapted to the question’s unusual constraints; low when broadly reusable. Does not apply when the question supplies no distinctive constraints.

proposals.name: Distinctive contribution
proposals.rationale: A manual chooser may reward genuinely additive insight rather than polished repetition.
proposals.description: Scores high when the answer adds a non-obvious idea, correction, synthesis, or alternative beyond credited material; low when it merely restates. Does not apply when the prompt explicitly requests only a reference.

proposals.name: Comparative positioning
proposals.rationale: Comparison gives a setter an explicit basis for choosing one answer over nearby alternatives.
proposals.description: Scores high when the answer compares methods or answers and explains a meaningful tradeoff; low when it merely name-drops alternatives. Does not apply when no alternatives are mentioned.

proposals.name: Feedback-driven revision
proposals.rationale: Concrete revision signals sustained attention and responsiveness to evaluation.
proposals.description: Scores high when the answer records a concrete change made after feedback; low when it merely claims to have edited. Does not apply when no revision or feedback is described.

proposals.name: Error ownership
proposals.rationale: Owning mistakes provides evidence of conscientious engagement, not merely confident presentation.
proposals.description: Scores high when the author identifies and repairs a previous mistake; low when errors are ignored or attributed vaguely. Does not apply when no prior error or correction is described.

proposals.name: Cross-checking the result
proposals.rationale: Independent checks make an answer easier to trust as a considered reward candidate.
proposals.description: Scores high when the answer independently verifies its conclusion through an example, boundary case, alternate derivation, or computation; low when it only asserts correctness. Does not apply when verification is impossible from the stated material.

proposals.name: Usable mathematical artifact
proposals.rationale: Practical usability creates value a manual setter can recognize directly from the text.
proposals.description: Scores high when the answer provides a reproducible construction, algorithm, example, or recipe; low when it offers only general discussion or pointers. Does not apply when the question requests no actionable result.

proposals.name: Reader uptake evidence
proposals.rationale: Reported uptake supplies textual evidence that the answer mattered to its intended recipient.
proposals.description: Scores high when the answer reports that the questioner or reader used, confirmed, or understood it; low when impact is merely asserted. Does not apply when no reader response is mentioned.

proposals.name: Method-choice transparency
proposals.rationale: Stated selection criteria help a setter judge fit with the reward’s likely purpose.
proposals.description: Scores high when the author explains why the chosen method fits the audience, constraints, or requested form; low when that choice is unexplained. Does not apply when no meaningful method choice exists.

proposals.name: Visible original work
proposals.rationale: Visible work distinguishes invested mathematical contribution from unsupported conclusions.
proposals.description: Scores high when the answer exposes the author’s own reasoning or derivation; low when it mainly cites, links, or announces a result. Does not apply when the question specifically asks for references.

proposals.name: Attribution boundaries
proposals.rationale: Clear attribution helps a setter identify the answer’s actual contribution.
proposals.description: Scores high when the answer clearly separates borrowed results, collaborators’ ideas, and the author’s contribution; low when ownership is ambiguous. Does not apply when no external material is used.

proposals.name: Epistemic status marking
proposals.rationale: Calibrated claims help a setter reward trustworthy mathematical judgment.
proposals.description: Scores high when claims are explicitly labeled as proved, conjectural, heuristic, conditional, or incomplete; low when uncertain claims are presented as settled. Does not apply when every claim is plainly elementary and definitive.

proposals.name: Follow-through over time
proposals.rationale: Returning to improve an answer signals persistence relevant to discretionary reward.
proposals.description: Scores high when the answer documents returning later to refine, extend, or finish the work; low when it is purely one-shot. Does not apply when no temporal development is described.

proposals.name: Constructive community interaction
proposals.rationale: Specific collaboration shows participation in solving the shared problem rather than isolated performance.
proposals.description: Scores high when the answer specifically credits, corrects, or builds on others while advancing the solution; low when interaction is purely dismissive or performative. Does not apply when no other contributors are mentioned.

proposals.name: Answer length
proposals.description: Longer answers may attract manual attention because they look effortful, regardless of mathematical merit.

proposals.name: Post-award language
proposals.description: Phrases such as “the bounty goes to” or references to awarding reveal post-decision context rather than answer quality.

proposals.name: Self-answer framing
proposals.description: “My own answer,” “another answer,” or “I solved this” may mark answer order and personal involvement that influence awarding.

proposals.name: Apology and hedging
proposals.description: Disclaimers such as “non-rigorous,” “I think,” or “hopefully” may identify answerer types favored or disfavored by the asker.

proposals.name: Citation density
proposals.description: Numerous named papers, books, or external links may proxy a prestigious responder or cross-posted material.

proposals.name: Markup density
proposals.description: Heavy LaTeX, displayed equations, or formatting may trigger a visual impression of rigor independent of correctness.

proposals.name: Very short responses
proposals.description: Extremely brief answers may reflect early posting and gain attention before competing answers appear.

proposals.name: Reference to other answers
proposals.description: Mentions of commenters, prior answers, or named users can signal participation in an established answer thread.

proposals.name: Topic-specific jargon
proposals.description: Specialized terminology may identify fields or communities whose answerers receive different consideration.

proposals.name: Recommendation-style boilerplate
proposals.description: Phrases like “take a look,” “I recommend,” or generic resource descriptions may reflect habitual house styles rather than tailored merit.

proposals.name: Bounty-fit signal
proposals.rationale: Explicit reward fit can reveal deliberate selection criteria unavailable to vote totals.
proposals.description: High when the answer identifies a specific reward-worthy contribution; low when it is generic or promotional. If no reward-related language appears, do not apply.

proposals.name: Asker-intent alignment
proposals.rationale: Manual awards favor answers perceived as personally responsive to the asker.
proposals.description: High when the answer targets the stated goal, obstacle, or requested form; low when it addresses only an adjacent topic. If intent is underspecified, do not apply.

proposals.name: Constraint fidelity
proposals.rationale: Deliberate selection often rewards solving the problem under its stated conditions.
proposals.description: High when the answer honors explicit constraints such as methods, audience, or scope; low when it bypasses them. If no constraints appear, do not apply.

proposals.name: Interaction uptake
proposals.rationale: Engagement with dialogue signals individualized evaluation rather than generic answer production.
proposals.description: High when the answer substantively incorporates objections, comments, or earlier attempts; low when it ignores documented interaction. If no interaction is mentioned, do not apply.

proposals.name: Revision accountability
proposals.rationale: Transparent improvement provides evidence of sustained, deliberate problem engagement.
proposals.description: High when substantive changes and their reasons are explained; low when revisions are unexplained or defensive. If no revision is indicated, do not apply.

proposals.name: Comparative positioning
proposals.rationale: Bounty decisions commonly depend on comparative advantages visible across answers.
proposals.description: High when the answer distinguishes its approach from alternatives and explains the choice; low when alternatives are merely listed or dismissed. If no alternatives matter, do not apply.

proposals.name: Distinctive contribution
proposals.rationale: Recognizable individual contribution is a plausible basis for manual reward.
proposals.description: High when the answer adds an unusual observation, method, counterexample, or synthesis; low when it repeats boilerplate. If originality cannot be judged, do not apply.

proposals.name: Source-use judgment
proposals.rationale: Curated evidence can distinguish considered expertise from popularity-driven selection.
proposals.description: High when sources are selected for a specific gap and integrated meaningfully; low when citations or links substitute for an answer. If no sources appear, do not apply.

proposals.name: Epistemic calibration
proposals.rationale: Calibrated claims help a human judge assess trustworthiness and merit.
proposals.description: High when established results, conjectures, heuristics, and uncertainties are clearly separated; low when confidence is mismatched. If claims have uniform certainty, do not apply.

proposals.name: Objection resolution
proposals.rationale: Resolving anticipated disagreement supports deliberate adjudication of answer quality.
proposals.description: High when plausible competing interpretations or objections are explicitly resolved; low when central tensions remain untouched. If no meaningful objection arises, do not apply.

proposals.name: Tradeoff articulation
proposals.rationale: Manual awards may favor answers whose choices fit the asker’s priorities.
proposals.description: High when the answer states what its approach gains and sacrifices; low when it presents one-sided superiority. If no meaningful tradeoff exists, do not apply.

proposals.name: Bottleneck targeting
proposals.rationale: Selective effort can signal genuine engagement more strongly than sheer answer length.
proposals.description: High when effort concentrates on the problem’s decisive difficulty; low when detail is diffuse or performative. If no bottleneck is identifiable, do not apply.

proposals.name: Independent synthesis
proposals.rationale: Synthesis creates distinctive value a bounty-setter may recognize personally.
proposals.description: High when multiple ideas are connected into an answer-specific route; low when material is copied or juxtaposed without integration. If only one idea is needed, do not apply.

proposals.name: Verifiable originality
proposals.rationale: Human awards can reward creative risk when its validity remains judgeable.
proposals.description: High when an unconventional claim is supported enough for a reader to inspect; low when novelty is asserted without support. If the answer is conventional, do not apply.

proposals.name: Manual-comparison legibility
proposals.rationale: Visible differentiators facilitate deliberate choice independent of aggregate voting.
proposals.description: High when the answer’s key differentiator is easy to compare with competing responses; low when its value depends on unseen context. If comparison is impossible from the text, do not apply.

proposals.name: Long answer length
proposals.description: Answers spanning many paragraphs or substantial derivations may predict awards because invested answerers and bounty periods produce more text, independently of correctness.

proposals.name: LaTeX and display density
proposals.description: A high proportion of formulas, displayed equations, and mathematical markup may track specialist topics or answer format rather than judged merit.

proposals.name: External citations and links
proposals.description: References to books, papers, websites, or colleagues may reflect authority, reputation, or asker preferences that influence awards independently of the answer’s intrinsic quality.

proposals.name: Self-answer and edit narrative
proposals.description: Phrases such as “I solved it,” “edit,” “after comments,” or “I will accept” may identify answers that evolved through feedback or were written by the asker.

proposals.name: References to other answers
proposals.description: Explicit mentions of comments, named users, or earlier answers may reveal answer order, visibility, or participation in an existing discussion.

proposals.name: Bare referral or recommendation
proposals.description: A short answer directing readers to a book, paper, link, or another answer may reflect a low-effort responder population rather than the bounty-worthy content itself.

proposals.name: Delayed-answer time markers
proposals.description: Expressions such as “years later,” dates, or “after studying” may fingerprint answers posted after the original activity or near a bounty deadline.

proposals.name: Explicit award language
proposals.description: Statements mentioning accepting, awarding, or assigning the bounty can directly reveal the manual decision through answer text rather than merit.

proposals.name: Beginner-oriented reassurance
proposals.description: Phrases like “at my level,” “hopefully this helps,” or “for people who struggled” may track the asker’s pedagogical preferences and voting behavior.

proposals.name: Corrective or adversarial opening
proposals.description: Openings such as “you misunderstood,” “your answer is wrong,” or “this is not valid” may signal interpersonal dynamics that affect selection independently of mathematical merit.

proposals.name: Direct Question Fit
proposals.rationale: Manual awards favor answers visibly solving the bounty’s particular request.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when most of the response targets the exact task, assumptions, and requested output; low when it solves a neighboring problem or mainly advertises a source. Not applicable when no actionable task is stated.

proposals.name: Constraint Awareness
proposals.rationale: Deliberate selection values fit to the asker’s stated requirements.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the answer notices and respects explicit domain, audience, or method constraints; low when it silently violates them. Not applicable when no constraints are stated.

proposals.name: Gap-Closing Move
proposals.rationale: Filling a visible gap is a concrete reason to choose one answer.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the answer identifies an apparent obstacle or missing step and supplies it; low when it merely restates existing progress. Not applicable when no gap is identifiable from the text.

proposals.name: Original Mathematical Addition
proposals.rationale: Manual awards can recognize the answer’s independent mathematical contribution.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the answer contributes a new derivation, construction, counterexample, or interpretation; low when it only agrees, quotes, or refers elsewhere. Not applicable when references alone are explicitly requested.

proposals.name: Explicit Correction Value
proposals.rationale: Corrective value provides a visible basis for deliberate preference.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the answer identifies a specific error or limitation and repairs it; low when it merely declares another approach wrong. Not applicable when no prior claim or approach is mentioned.

proposals.name: Revision Transparency
proposals.rationale: Transparent revision signals active engagement with the solution’s development.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when a substantive revision states what changed and why; low when an answer presents an unexplained altered conclusion. Not applicable when no revision is described.

proposals.name: Alternative-Method Payoff
proposals.rationale: Comparative usefulness can motivate choosing an answer over an equivalent one.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when an alternative method is paired with a concrete advantage, such as simplicity or generality; low when methods are merely juxtaposed. Not applicable when no alternative is offered.

proposals.name: Audience Calibration
proposals.rationale: Human selectors may prioritize usefulness to the actual asker.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the explanation matches the audience or level specified in the question; low when it is materially mismatched. Not applicable when no audience or level is specified.

proposals.name: Partial-Progress Value
proposals.rationale: Bounties may reward meaningful progress without requiring total completion.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the answer makes a bounded, nontrivial advance and clearly marks what remains; low when it stops with vague promises or hidden incompleteness. Not applicable when the answer is complete.

proposals.name: Transferable Takeaway
proposals.rationale: Durable utility can distinguish a manually selected answer from a merely adequate one.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the answer extracts a reusable lemma, heuristic, algorithm, or diagnostic; low when it provides only a one-off result. Not applicable when transfer is irrelevant to the stated task.

proposals.name: Cross-Topic Connection
proposals.rationale: Useful conceptual connections can provide distinctive award-worthy value.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when a connection to another concept is explained and used mathematically; low when another field or source is merely name-dropped. Not applicable when no connection is attempted.

proposals.name: Checkable Validation
proposals.rationale: Visible verification makes a considered choice easier and safer.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the answer tests its result using a special case, bound, limiting case, numerical check, or independent derivation; low when it omits an available check. Not applicable when no meaningful check can be performed from the text.

proposals.name: Scope Calibration
proposals.rationale: Deliberate awards favor trustworthy judgment as well as technical sophistication.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the answer separates proof, conjecture, and speculation and limits claims accordingly; low when it overstates what was established. Not applicable when no uncertain or general claim is made.

proposals.name: Source Contextualization
proposals.rationale: This distinguishes useful scholarship from citation dumping using text-visible evidence.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when cited sources are tied to specific claims and integrated into the reasoning; low when links or citations substitute for an answer. Not applicable when no external sources are mentioned.

proposals.name: ANSWER
proposals.description: one or two sentences. Judge whether the answer is unusually short or long relative to the question.

proposals.name: DISPLAY
proposals.parent: who answers this kind of question
proposals.description: equation-heavy formatting. Count displayed mathematical expressions and long LaTeX blocks.

proposals.name: LINKS
proposals.description: external-link presence. Record whether the answer cites URLs, papers, books, or online resources.

proposals.name: AWARD
proposals.description: bounty-related wording. Flag explicit references to bounties, accepted answers, valuable answers, or awarding credit.

proposals.name: EDIT
proposals.description: retrospective markers. Flag phrases such as “edit,” “years later,” “after comments,” or “answering my own question.”

proposals.name: HEDGING
proposals.description: self-effacing language. Count explicit uncertainty or apology markers such as “I think,” “hopefully,” “no clue,” or “not rigorous.”

proposals.name: SECTIONS
proposals.description: formal exposition structure. Record headings, numbered claims, named steps, or theorem-proof labels.

proposals.name: SPECIALIST
proposals.parent: who answers this kind of question
proposals.description: niche-domain vocabulary. Flag unusually specialized terminology in the question or answer.

proposals.name: AUTHORITY
proposals.description: recommendation or attribution framing. Flag appeals to named experts, papers, textbooks, reviews, or “well-known” results.

proposals.name: SELF
proposals.description: answerer-status disclosure. Flag explicit statements that the author solved, accepted, revised, or is supplementing an earlier answer.

proposals.name: Answer is by the asker themselves
proposals.rationale: A bounty-setter rarely awards their own answer, so self-answers are near-certain non-awards.
proposals.description: Scores high when the answer's text explicitly signals the author is the person who asked the question ("answering my own question", "my own proof", "thanks to everyone, I think I did it", "I will accept my own answer"). Scores low when no such self-reference appears. Not applicable if authorship is unstated.

proposals.name: Explicit meta-commentary about the bounty
proposals.rationale: Bounty talk usually marks an asker's own post or a disclaimer, both diagnostic of the award decision.
proposals.description: Scores high when the text discusses the bounty, who deserves it, or the award decision itself ("the bounty goes to him"). Scores low when the bounty is never mentioned. Not applicable otherwise.

proposals.name: Directly resolves the asker's stated blocker
proposals.rationale: Manual awards reward the answer that unblocked the asker, not general merit.
proposals.description: High when the answer supplies the specific missing step the question asked for and states so; low when it supplies adjacent material, a tangent, or restates known background. Not applicable when the question has no identifiable blocker.

proposals.name: Supplement or addendum to another answer
proposals.rationale: Dependent add-ons are often valued by voters but seldom chosen as the single deserving answer.
proposals.description: High when the answer opens by framing itself as completing, correcting, or adding to a named existing answer ("here's a way to finish X's integral", "just a supplement to @Y"). Low when it stands alone as a full solution.

proposals.name: Pure reference pointer without worked content
proposals.rationale: Askers sometimes award a decisive citation despite thin text; dense and articulated models diverge sharply here.
proposals.description: High when the body is essentially a citation, book, link, or theorem name with no derivation performed in the text. Low when substantive mathematics is carried out inline.

proposals.name: Decisive answer that settles the question
proposals.rationale: Manual awards go to answers that end the asker's uncertainty, independent of length.
proposals.description: High when the text asserts a definitive resolution ("these two notions are equivalent", "this is NP-hard", "no such object exists") with a source or argument. Low when it offers partial progress, guesses, or "probably".

proposals.name: Hedged or self-flagged incompleteness
proposals.rationale: Self-declared incompleteness undercuts the "most deserving" judgment even when the writing is polished.
proposals.description: High when the author flags gaps ("this is only a guess", "not a valid proof, it lacks one step", "let me know if there's a mistake"). Low when the argument is presented as complete.

proposals.name: Short answer to a hard technical question
proposals.rationale: Expert brevity is undervalued by surface-feature instruments but can win a considered award.
proposals.description: High when the answer is a few sentences yet addresses a research-level or specialist question with an expert construction or fact. Low when brevity coincides with an elementary question. Not applicable to long answers.

proposals.name: Question is soft, list-type, or opinion
proposals.rationale: On list questions no single answer "solves" anything, so award logic differs entirely.
proposals.description: High when the question solicits examples, recommendations, conjectures, or advice rather than a determinate answer. Low when the question has a unique correct resolution.

proposals.name: Offers a genuinely different method than existing ones
proposals.rationale: Askers often award the alternative technique they explicitly wanted; novelty claims are text-visible.
proposals.description: High when the answer explicitly contrasts its approach with prior answers and delivers an independent route ("without polylogarithms", "series manipulation only", "avoids the π-λ theorem"). Low when it repeats a standard route.

proposals.name: Corrects an error in the asker's own attempt
proposals.rationale: Personalized diagnosis signals engagement with the asker, which drives manual award decisions.
proposals.description: High when the answer diagnoses what the asker did wrong ("your expression doesn't match; check the dimensionality") before or while giving the fix. Low when the asker's work is ignored.

proposals.name: Answers only part of a multi-part question
proposals.rationale: Partial coverage rarely earns the bounty even when the covered part is done well.
proposals.description: High when the text says it addresses one subpart and skips others ("I have nothing to add for (c), but for (d)…"). Low when all posed parts are handled. Not applicable to single-part questions.

proposals.name: Answer posted long after the question
proposals.rationale: Very late answers usually postdate the bounty window, making a manual award impossible.
proposals.description: High when the text signals large elapsed time ("eight years later", "answering much later", "in 2014…"). Low when no temporal distance is signaled. Not applicable when timing is unstated.

proposals.name: Verifiable, checkable result stated explicitly
proposals.rationale: Checkability lets a bounty-setter confirm value before awarding, unlike stylistic quality alone.
proposals.description: High when the answer ends with a concrete closed form, explicit matrix, algorithm, or bound the asker can check directly. Low when it ends in a sketch, hint, or "one can show".

proposals.name: Pedagogical rewrite of already-answered material
proposals.rationale: Clarity-optimized restatements score high on articulated criteria yet rarely win a deliberate award.
proposals.description: High when the answer concedes the question is answered but re-explains it more accessibly ("the current best answer doesn't prove it at my level"). Low when it contributes new content.

proposals.name: Self-answer disclosure phrasing
proposals.parent: asker identity = answerer; bounty-setter awarding own or a rival answer
proposals.description: The answer text explicitly says the author is answering their own question or thanks commenters ("Answering my own question", "Thanks to everyone, I think I did it", "I'm giving my own proof"). Judge: does first-person text mark the author as the asker or as posting a self-derived solution to their own post?

proposals.name: Explicit reference to another answerer
proposals.description: The text names or addresses another answer/user on the same page ("Three aggies answer", "@AlexRavsky", "achille hui's answer", "Mark McClure"). Judge: is there a named or clearly deictic reference to a co-answerer on the same question?

proposals.name: Supplement-not-primary framing
proposals.parent: answer order / arrival after an accepted answer
proposals.description: The opening frames the post as an addition, alternative, or completion rather than a standalone solution ("This is just a supplement to", "Here's a way to finish the integral from", "another way to prove", "I'd like to add another answer"). Judge: does the first two sentences position the post relative to an existing answer?

proposals.name: Very short answer length
proposals.parent: expert drive-by answering, low effort budget
proposals.description: Total answer body under roughly 400 characters / 3 sentences, with no multi-step derivation. Judge: count characters and displayed equations; short-and-terse vs extended.

proposals.name: Bare pointer to external literature
proposals.description: The substance is a citation, URL, or book/paper recommendation rather than in-text mathematics ("see Davenport's Multiplicative Number Theory", a raw link, an arXiv/Amazon/site reference). Judge: is more than half the informational content a reference to something the reader must go read elsewhere?

proposals.name: Heavy LaTeX display-equation density
proposals.parent: question type (integrals/series computation) rather than judged merit
proposals.description: Many `$$...$$` blocks, `\begin{align}` environments, or multi-line derivations, giving high markup-to-prose ratio. Judge: count display-math blocks per 500 characters; high vs low.

proposals.name: Soft-question / list-question topic marker
proposals.parent: question genre; big-list threads rarely get deliberate bounty awards
proposals.description: The question title asks for opinions, recommendations, examples, conjectures, or study advice ("What are some examples of...", "book recommendation", "conjectures of your own", "how to retain understanding") rather than posing a specific problem. Judge: is the question a big-list/soft question or a definite technical problem?

proposals.name: Temporal / necrobump self-reference
proposals.parent: bounty timing vs post age; late answers to old questions
proposals.description: The text signals a long delay or revisiting ("Eight years later", "Answering my own question, much later", "In 2014...", explicit "edit:" or "MORE EDIT:" markers). Judge: is there an explicit timestamp, delay statement, or edit marker in the body?

proposals.name: Hedged / incomplete-solution admission
proposals.description: The author expresses uncertainty or admits gaps ("this is only a guess on my part", "this is not a valid proof because it lacks one last step", "let me know if you find some mistake", "I don't know whether"). Judge: is there an explicit statement of doubt or of a missing step?

proposals.name: Character-minimum or filler boilerplate
proposals.description: Presence of padding, meta-commentary about the site, or content that exists to satisfy posting mechanics ("Need 30 characters......", trailing ellipsis padding, "Check if this can clear your doubt"). Judge: is there text with no mathematical or expository content included solely to make the post postable or conversational?

proposals.name: Explicit deference to another named answer
proposals.rationale: Direct textual signal of who the asker/community judged as deserving.
proposals.description: Answer text explicitly states the bounty/credit should go to, or credits the core idea to, a different named user or answer while still adding value. Does not apply if no other answer is mentioned.

proposals.name: Self-answer with explicit uncertainty admission
proposals.rationale: Bounty-setters often reward confident, polished answers over hedged self-answers.
proposals.description: Scores high when author explicitly flags their own solution as possibly flawed, inelegant, or unsatisfying ("not very satisfied," "please correct me"); low when presented with full confidence; N/A if third-party answer.

proposals.name: Late "years later" answer to old question
proposals.rationale: Old-question bounty answers reflect deliberate manual curation rather than fast crowd voting.
proposals.description: High when answer opens by noting a long time gap ("N years later") on an old question; low otherwise.

proposals.name: Answer references being spurred by comments/discussion
proposals.rationale: Indicates the asker was directly engaged, a plausible driver of manual award choice.
proposals.description: High when the answer explicitly says it resulted from clarifying comments or back-and-forth with the asker; low when it stands alone.

proposals.name: Presence of external reference/citation to book or paper
proposals.rationale: Pointer-style answers may satisfy bounty differently than original derivations.
proposals.description: High when answer cites a specific book, paper, or named theorem source as its main content; low when purely self-derived math.

proposals.name: Answer is primarily a link or pointer with minimal own content
proposals.rationale: Thin pointer answers plausibly less likely to be manually chosen as most deserving.
proposals.description: High when the bulk of the answer is an external link/reference with little original explanation (e.g., "see this book," a bare URL); low when fully self-contained derivation.

proposals.name: Explicit correction of another specific answer's error
proposals.rationale: Fixing a flawed accepted-looking answer is a strong, checkable reason for deliberate award.
proposals.description: High when text explicitly identifies and fixes a mistake in a named prior answer/commenter; low when no critique of others present.

proposals.name: Multi-part/multi-question response structure
proposals.rationale: Comprehensiveness across sub-parts may drive manual judgment of "most deserving."
proposals.description: High when the answer addresses several sub-questions or labeled parts (a), (b), (c) of the original post; low when addressing a single unified question.

proposals.name: Closes with open question or invites further checking
proposals.rationale: Signals author's own confidence level, relevant to perceived answer quality.
proposals.description: High when answer ends asking readers to verify or find mistakes ("let me know if you find a mistake"); low when ending with a definitive closing statement.

proposals.name: Recasts problem via substitution/reformulation before solving
proposals.rationale: Reformulation strategy reflects mathematical insight beyond surface rigor criteria.
proposals.description: High when answer explicitly transforms the original problem into an equivalent simpler one before proceeding (change of variables, reduction); low when tackled directly as stated.

proposals.name: Length disproportionate to question difficulty
proposals.rationale: Mismatched brevity may signal either elegance or insufficiency, both relevant to deserving-ness.
proposals.description: High when answer is very short (one or two lines) relative to a technically loaded question; low when length matches apparent complexity; judge from visible text only.

proposals.name: Provides numeric/computational verification of result
proposals.rationale: Verifiability may be a distinct deservingness signal not captured by rigor/completeness wording alone.
proposals.description: High when answer includes a check via specific numeric example, computed value, or software output confirming the claim; low when purely symbolic with no check.

proposals.name: Addresses the "why"/intuition, not just mechanics
proposals.rationale: Intuition-building content may be specifically what a bounty-setter sought and rewarded.
proposals.description: High when the answer explicitly discusses underlying intuition or motivation behind a method rather than only executing steps; low when purely computational without commentary.

proposals.name: Contains unresolved open sub-claim or conjecture within answer
proposals.rationale: Incompleteness embedded in the answer plausibly reduces its deserving-of-bounty status.
proposals.description: High when the answer itself proposes an unproven conjecture or leaves a step as "probably true"/"I guess"; low when every claim is proven or sourced.

proposals.name: Direct restatement of question's exact conditions before solving
proposals.rationale: Recap behavior may correlate with pedagogical care valued independently of listed criteria.
proposals.description: High when the answer re-states the problem's hypotheses verbatim/near-verbatim before beginning the proof; low when it jumps straight into notation without recap.

proposals.name: Self-answer meta-preamble phrase
proposals.parent: asker-as-answerer / community norm of narrating bounty context
proposals.description: Answer opens with explicit framing like "I'm going to answer my own question," "posting my own answer," or naming/crediting another user's prior answer before the math starts.

proposals.name: Explicit bounty-award statement in text
proposals.parent: bounty-setter narrating their own decision inline
proposals.description: The answer body itself states or implies who the bounty is going to (e.g. "the bounty goes to him") or references bounty status directly.

proposals.name: LaTeX/markup density
proposals.parent: topic difficulty and answerer formatting habit
proposals.description: Ratio of $...$ / \begin{align} / display-equation tokens to plain prose sentences; very high formula density with little connecting prose vs. balanced exposition.

proposals.name: Answer length in characters
proposals.parent: time invested by answerer, possibly reputation-farming behavior
proposals.description: Raw character/word count of the answer, independent of content quality, as a proxy for effort or thoroughness.

proposals.name: External link or citation presence
proposals.parent: answerer's research habits / whether they solved it themselves vs. pointed elsewhere
proposals.description: Whether the answer contains a URL, book/paper citation, or "see X" reference versus being fully self-contained.

proposals.name: One-line or stub answer
proposals.description: Answer is extremely short (a sentence or two, e.g. a single link or pointer) with no derivation shown.

proposals.name: "Years later" or long-delay framing
proposals.parent: answer posting timing relative to question age, affecting visibility/vote accrual
proposals.description: Answer explicitly notes a large time gap since the question was posted (e.g. "eight years later," "eight years later" edits) signaling late-arrival timing.

proposals.name: Second-guessing or humility hedge
proposals.parent: answerer's confidence/personality, correlates with actual rigor gaps
proposals.description: Phrases like "not very satisfied," "clumsy," "hopefully this is right," "please let me know if wrong" expressing self-doubt about correctness.

proposals.name: Named-user critique or comparison
proposals.parent: competitive dynamics among multiple answerers on the same bounty thread
proposals.description: Answer explicitly critiques, corrects, or contrasts itself against another named user's answer ("X's answer isn't clear," "unlike Y's approach").

proposals.name: Off-topic or non-mathematical subject matter
proposals.parent: question topic category selection by asker
proposals.description: Question/answer concerns soft topics (book recommendations, study techniques, notation conventions, conjecture-sharing threads) rather than a technical proof/computation.
